_comment: Exact work counts for session-browser's retrieval hot paths. Generated by `python -m session_browser.perf_budget bless`; do not hand-edit. Any movement fails the suite on purpose -- see session_browser/perf_budget.py for why these are counts and not timings. _blessed records what this file's committed version says versus what is here now; it is derived, not written by hand, so it is the diff's own account of whether a regression was accepted -- and it survives being re-blessed.

guards.cli.search.absent: A term in no session must cost no parse and no load. Every session's entries are already cached, and the scan of that text -- not the parser, and not a read of the raw transcripts -- answers a miss.
guards.cli.search.absent.stateless: With the entry cache switched off, the raw files answer. A term in no session must cost zero canonical parses: the prefilter, not the parser, answers a miss.
guards.cli.search.rare: A warm entry cache leaves only genuine matches to load and nothing to parse. transcripts_parsed rising from zero means a session that had not changed was parsed again; entry_cache_loads rising towards the corpus means the scan of cached text was dropped; corpus_bytes_read rising above cli.list's means a raw transcript was read to answer a search the cache already could.
guards.cli.search.rare.cold: The first search of a history, nothing cached. Every file-backed session is parsed exactly once and stored, the build is routed to worker processes, and the search then loads only its matches. transcripts_parsed above the file session count means a session was parsed once to cache it and again to search it.
guards.cli.search.rare.appended: One transcript grew since it was cached, which is what a live session looks like. It alone is parsed again: transcripts_parsed and entry_cache_stores are both 1. More means a change to one file discarded what was known about the others.
guards.cli.search.rare.stateless: With the entry cache switched off, the raw files answer. The prefilter must rule out the corpus and leave only genuine candidates to parse. This is the number that grows to the whole corpus if the native scan is dropped.
guards.cli.search.rare.no_rg: With ripgrep unavailable, the in-process scan must read each cached text file exactly once and load only the candidates: entry_cache_bytes_read is every text file once plus the candidates' own pairs, never the text twice.
guards.cli.search.rare.no_rg.stateless: With the entry cache switched off, the raw files answer. With ripgrep unavailable too, the in-process byte prefilter must still read each candidate file exactly once, not once to partition and again to parse.
guards.cli.search.rare.role: --role narrows matches search already holds, so every counter must equal cli.search.rare's. A role filter that re-read a transcript to learn its roles, or that skipped the prefilter to classify candidates first, shows here as a rise over it.
guards.cli.search.common: The unavoidable upper bound -- a term in every session. Each session is loaded once and none is parsed, and above the threshold the loads are routed to worker processes.
guards.cli.search.common.limit: A term in every session, and --limit 5. The scan of cached text says which sessions match and discovery says when each was last active, so only the rows shown are loaded: entry_cache_loads is the file-backed sessions among those five, not the corpus. Rising towards cli.search.common's means --limit went back to bounding the output and not the work.
guards.cli.search.common.limit_many: The same with --limit 160, enough rows that loading them is routed to worker processes, as the unlimited search's loads are. process_pool_sessions falling to zero means a large limit loads on threads, which is slower than the search it replaced.
guards.cli.search.common.stateless: With the entry cache switched off, the raw files answer. The unavoidable upper bound -- a term in every session. Nothing may read the corpus more than once even when nothing is skipped.
guards.cli.search.claude: Provider scoping must confine the work to that provider: no SQLite connection is opened when opencode was not asked for, and no other provider's cached entries are scanned or loaded.
guards.cli.search.opencode: The thin raw-part scan must rule sessions out before the ordered join, so only survivors reach a canonical parse. OpenCode is never held in the entry cache: every cache counter stays zero.
guards.cli.search.opencode.v2: The same scan over OpenCode 2.x's schema: one thin raw pass over session_message before the ordered read, so only survivors are parsed. The v1 attempt each reader makes first must stay free -- rejected while preparing, it never counts as a statement.
guards.cli.search.pi: Pi transcripts are ordinary JSONL, so they are cached and scanned like the claude files. A parse here means Pi fell out of the entry cache; a load per session means it fell out of the scan.
guards.cli.search.pi.stateless: With the entry cache switched off, the raw files answer. Pi transcripts must be ruled out by the same candidate scan the claude files go through. A parse per session here means Pi fell out of the prefilter path.
guards.cli.search.grok: Grok sessions are discovered from three small files each (summary.json, the head and tail of updates.jsonl, events.jsonl), kept in the scan memo: warm, discovery_scans is zero. The transcript is ordinary JSONL, cached and scanned like the claude files; a parse here means Grok fell out of the entry cache.
guards.cli.search.grok.stateless: With the entry cache switched off, the raw files answer. Every Grok session is scanned once by discovery (discovery_scans is the session count) and its transcript ruled out by the same candidate scan the claude files go through; a parse per session means Grok fell out of the prefilter path.
guards.cli.search.codex_zst: Codex compresses old rollouts to .jsonl.zst. The first of these two searches reads each one once, decompressing it as it is parsed into the entry cache, and keeps no decompressed copy: zst_decompressions, which counts copies written, is zero, and corpus_file_opens and transcripts_parsed are the rollout count. The second -- a fresh process as far as either cache can tell -- must read and parse nothing. A copy per rollout here is five times its size on disk, kept for a parse that never comes back.
guards.cli.search.codex_zst.stateless: With the entry cache switched off, the raw files answer. Decompressing compressed rollouts per query cost ~1s over 684 real ones. Each must be decompressed once, into the on-disk cache, and the second of these two searches must read only the copies: zst_decompressions is the rollout count, not twice it.
guards.cli.list: Listing is metadata plus each returned session's entry count, and the count comes from one header line of the entry cache. It must never parse a transcript or load one, and its corpus reads must stay bounded by the discovery window rather than by session length: they equal cli.stats's.
guards.cli.list.cold: A listing over sessions nothing has cached reads each returned session once to count it, and keeps what it read: one parse and one store per row returned, none for the rows the limit dropped.
guards.cli.list.stateless: With the entry cache switched off, the raw files answer. A listing counts each returned session's entries by reading it once -- the returned rows only, never the corpus.
guards.cli.list.ending: --ending filters on how each session ended. Claude and Pi carry it from discovery's tail read, so only Codex sessions from its index are asked, and each rollout's answer is remembered: warm, ending_reads is zero and every Codex candidate is a scan_memo hit. Reads here mean the memo stopped holding, or the filter ran before the others and asked sessions it was going to drop.
guards.cli.list.ending.stateless: With the entry cache switched off, the raw files answer. With nothing remembered, --ending reads each Codex candidate's rollout once, from its end: ending_reads is the Codex session count, and ending_bytes_read a tail of each, not the rollouts whole.
guards.cli.list.preview: Ending previews must take each returned session's entries from the cache, once, and parse nothing: the count and the ending come from the same load.
guards.cli.list.preview.stateless: With the entry cache switched off, the raw files answer. Ending previews must reuse the listing's count scan, limited to the returned sessions, rather than load transcripts again.
guards.cli.list.no_codex_db: The file-scan fallback is the safety net for a missing or stale Codex index. It must stay budgeted so a regression in it cannot hide behind the DB fast path. It is also the only workload that reads rollout files, so it is where a Codex vocabulary the head or tail scan no longer recognises shows up -- as a rise, since finding no turn means reading the whole file to discover it.
guards.cli.list.codex_db_stale: A Codex index lacking one rollout must cost that rollout's read and no more: corpus_file_opens is cli.list's plus one file's worth. Codex leaves some rollouts unindexed for good, and when a gap fell back to scanning the whole tree it put ~1.5 s on every call on a real machine. If this rises to cli.list.no_codex_db's opens, the whole-tree fallback is back.
guards.cli.calls.absent: calls finds its sessions through search's scan: a pattern in no session loads nothing and parses nothing, whatever the corpus holds.
guards.cli.calls.rare: calls must load only the scan's candidates, and once each: the call's output is paired from the entries the search already holds, never by reading a transcript again.
guards.cli.calls.rare.stateless: With the entry cache switched off, the raw files answer. calls must parse only the prefilter's candidates, and once each: the call's output is paired from the entries the search already holds, never by reading a transcript again.
guards.cli.calls.common: A pattern in every session: calls keeps every candidate's entries to pair outputs, so this pins how many sessions a broad pattern loads and that it still reads each one once.
guards.cli.list.codex_rewound: A rewound Codex thread's earlier files are attached by name and never opened in discovery: every counter equals cli.list's. The gap reader used to open each one, decompressing a 39 MB first file on a real machine, only to drop it for a known id.
guards.cli.search.codex_rewound: A phrase said only before a rewind lives only in a file the index does not name. The thread's cached entries span every one of its files, so the scan finds the phrase and exactly the one thread is loaded; zero loads means text said before a rewind is unsearchable again.
guards.cli.search.codex_rewound.stateless: With the entry cache switched off, the raw files answer. A phrase said only before a rewind lives only in a file the index does not name. The prefilter must scan that file too and send exactly the one thread to a parse; zero parses means text said before a rewind is unsearchable again.
guards.cli.stats: Statistics come from discovery metadata alone, and discovery remembers what it read from each Claude and Pi transcript: with nothing changed, no transcript is opened at all -- discovery_scans is zero and scan_memo_hits is every such file. What is left in corpus_bytes_read is what no memo covers.
guards.cli.stats.cold: The first discovery of a history: each Claude and Pi transcript is opened once, for its head and its tail, and remembered. discovery_scans above the file count means one was read twice.
guards.cli.stats.appended: One transcript grew since the last discovery. It alone is opened again: discovery_scans is 1.
guards.cli.stats.stateless: With the entry cache switched off, the raw files answer. Statistics come from discovery metadata alone: no transcript may be parsed to produce them, and the read volume is bounded by the discovery window, not by session length.
guards.cli.get: Retrieving a session whose entries are cached must load it once and parse nothing, on top of the discovery pass that located it.
guards.cli.get.cold: Retrieving one session nothing has cached must read one transcript, on top of the discovery pass that located it, and store it: one parse, one store, and no load.
guards.cli.get.recent: A recent conversation and its text budget must use one load of the session's entries, not separate user and assistant retrievals.
guards.tui.search.rare: The progress readout the TUI displays. Callback volume is capped by design -- per session and per 4096 database rows, never per row or per entry.
guards.tui.search.rare.stateless: With the entry cache switched off, the raw files answer. The progress readout must observe the scan the CLI runs, not re-walk it: its corpus reads equal cli.search.rare.stateless's.
guards.tui.search.unordered: The TUI's words wave. It must load each candidate ONCE, in one scan for all the typed words together, after one native scan of the cached text per word has narrowed the sessions -- never a loading scan per word. The key keeps its old name so a bless shows this workload's counters moving rather than a new workload.
guards.tui.search.unordered.stateless: With the entry cache switched off, the raw files answer. The words wave must parse each candidate ONCE, in one scan for all the typed words together, after one native candidate scan per word has narrowed the files -- never a parsing scan per word, which would read the corpus once for each word typed.
guards.lib.search.process_route: The ids/snippets shape above the candidate threshold must be routed to worker processes, and the ruled-out majority must not be sent with it.
guards.lib.search.process_route.stateless: With the entry cache switched off, the raw files answer. The ids/snippets shape above the candidate threshold must be routed to worker processes, and the prefiltered-out majority must not be sent with it.
guards.lib.search.keep_entries: The entries-retaining shape must stay in this process: shipping whole transcripts back from workers would pickle the corpus.
guards.lib.search.keep_entries.stateless: With the entry cache switched off, the raw files answer. The entries-retaining shape must stay in this process: shipping whole transcripts back from workers would pickle the corpus.

loop_guards.loop.parse_jsonl: The per-line decode loop. Anything added per line is multiplied by every line of every transcript read -- this is where a context manager per line (contextlib.suppress over try/except, measured at 4.85x) or an extra attribute lookup actually costs.
loop_guards.loop.claude_tool_entries: Claude's tool_use and tool_result branches, most of an agent session's records and outside loop.parse_jsonl's user-text input. Each block's metadata carries the call id that pairs it (measured at ~40 ns a block); more per block is paid on every tool record of every Claude transcript read.
loop_guards.loop.ticking_rows: The opencode row loop, which reads the entire part table. row_tick_wrappers pins that the wrapper exists; this pins what one row through it costs.
loop_guards.loop.find_entry_matches: The offsets loop, including its every-1024 cancellation gate. The gate must stay cheap: it runs on every hit, and a cancelled() call moved out of its mask would run on every one.
loop_guards.loop.count_overlapping: The match-counting scan. Its body is a str.find and an integer add; anything else added here runs once per match in the corpus.
loop_guards.loop.raw_text_may_match: The byte-prefilter's escape decoding, run over raw text before any parse. It decides whether a file is read at all, so work added here is paid on sessions that never match.
loop_guards.loop.codex_entries: The Codex record loop and the dedupe generator behind it. Codex is the largest provider in a real corpus, so a comparison added to the branch dispatch is paid on every record of every rollout read -- including the reasoning and tool records that never produce a user-visible entry.
loop_guards.loop.codex_db_rows: Per-row Session construction in the Codex DB fast path. One dataclass per index row per discovery; anything added inside this loop is paid once per Codex session, per run.
